root: ^this badger is pretty young, despite his cane and obvious limping when he moves around. Always happy to chitchat, he's a warm person.

s: ^Hi, I'm the train conductor, what's your name?

c-0: ^Mykola Tymchenko, at your service. Don’t worry, I’m not one of those passengers who touches things he shouldn’t. Used to fix these beasts for a living.
^All my life. My father too. Guess it runs in the oil, eh eh !  If something rattles or hisses, I’ll hear it before the gauge does, don't worry about it, chief.
^Damn right I am. Any mechanic that respect themself should take their work seriously.  People forget these machines carry lives, not just cargo.

c-1: ^Could be worse. My leg complains, but at least I can sit down for once.

c-0: ^Yeah. Fell off a maintenance platform a few years ago. The ground won. Doctors said it kept me out of the army. Me wife calls it good luck.
^Only when it rains, when I walk and stand too much or when the brakes squeal too long.

s: ^come on, your going to be ok, Mykola. I'll make sure of it. Ok ?
^no, don't do this to me, Mykola. Not the dying speech.

c-0: ^He laugh for a few seconds yeah right, we will see I guess.
c-1: ^If I don't make it, go to my family. Tell them everything. At the back of this photograph is there adress. If I die, take it and go see them. Ok ?

c-0: ^Thank you chief. He gently tap your arm.

s: ^no I won't because your going to live, ok ?

c-0: ^He sigh I will try my best, but if I don't make it, I'm counting on you.
^If I don't make it, go to my family. Tell them everything. At the back of this photograph is there adress. If I die, take it and go see them. Ok ?

s: ^no I won't because your going to live, ok ?

c-0: ^Thank you chief. He gently tap your arm.
c-1: ^He sigh I will try my best, but if I don't make it, I'm counting on you.

c-0: ^From a small workshop town south of Khoren. Smelled like gas, metal swarf and cabbage soup, but it was home.

s: ^wait you worked on the railroad fortresses of Khoren ?! I heard of these giant machines of war. That must have been something !
^it's in the northern steppes, if I recall. People have it bad, I heard.

c-0: ^Yes I did. He sound really proud of himself. I worked on assembling the weel system, not an easy work for something weighting like eight fully loaded trains.
c-1: ^You heard well, but not from us. We are not the complaining type, you see. Yes the work is hard and the pay is cheap, but we work like a big family. If only you could see the joyful atmosphere in the workshop!

s: ^it sound like a lot of fun.

c-0: ^A bomb is what happened. A gas one. We had to run leave quickly the town. SRUR soldiers were waiting in the wood. It was a slaughter. His joyful attitude change to a serious tone. If it wasn't for this damn leg, I would have headed for  Akhilla to join up with our army.
c-1: ^•	what's bringing you aboard my train ?
^My family's waiting for me in the neutral zone. I stayed behind too long, thought I could earn a bit more for my girls.

s: ^why kind of jobs did you do in the meantime?

c-0: ^They could flee faster than me with the armoured trucks of our army. I on the other hand had the chance to play hide and seek for a few days with the raïshurians. Lot of fun.
c-1: ^Scrapping old engines, fixing what was left. People still need trains, even in hell
c-2: ^Sure thing! He brings out his wallet, where a small worn photograph show Mykola with a woman and a young girl. My wife, Olena. tough as steel. And our little miracle, Sofiika. Five years old.

c-0: ^Like a fish in the desert miss water. But they’re safe, and that’s all a man can ask for now.
c-1: ^I received a few letters when I was still working. It was mostly me who sent letters. But the next time I hear from them, it will be from their own mouth. He smile happily just imagining it.

s: ^what will you do once in the neutral zone?

c-0: ^I don't intend to really change anything in my life, just do it somewhere else. I'll find work easely. Mechanics are still needed, even where the guns don’t reach. And I could by a bike to Soffika and teach her how to ride it.

^Mykola’s overalls are patched but clean. His claws are dark with grease, and his movements are practiced — efficient without rush. His limp is noticeable, but he hides it with humor.  His eyes light up when talking about machines, dim slightly when war or family are mentioned.
^He is a good man, loving of others.
